title: Transistors and signal amplification
summary: Explains how NPN and PNP transistors are constructed and operate, and how they are used for switching and for signal amplification in a transistor amplifier circuit.

sections.heading: Transistor construction
paragraphs: The transistor (Transfer-Resistance) is a development of the diode. Instead of a single P-N junction, a transistor has two junctions, either N-P-N or P-N-P, usually called NPN or PNP. NPN types are by far the most common.
bullets: NPN is by far the most common

sections.heading: Operation of NPN and PNP transistors
paragraphs: A transistor needs a stable dc supply. With 0V on the base of an NPN transistor there is no current between collector and emitter. When the base is 0.6V higher than the emitter, a current flows between collector and emitter.

In the example circuit, R1/R2 provide 0.6V on the base, so a small current flows through the base/emitter PN junction. This causes a much larger current through the collector/emitter. R3 limits the current to prevent overload and produces a voltage drop that gives the output voltage Vout.
A PNP type works the same way, but the dc supply must be reversed and the base voltage must be 0.6V lower than the emitter for a collector current to flow.
bullets: NPN: base 0.6V higher than emitter for collector current
PNP: base 0.6V lower than emitter, supply reversed
A small base current controls a much larger collector current

sections.heading: Switching and amplification
paragraphs: For switching, the transistor is biased either fully off (no current flow) or fully on (maximum current flow).

For amplification, the transistor is biased 'half on'. An alternating signal (audio, video, sensor output) applied to the base adds to and subtracts from the dc bias voltage. This causes a large change in collector current, producing a voltage swing across the collector load resistor (R3). Amplifiers boost signals from sensors such as temperature sensors, photodiodes and electromagnetic tacho generators.
bullets: Switching: biased off or fully on
Example: a 10mV input gives typically 100mV to 150mV output

sections.heading: The transistor amplifier circuit
paragraphs: When a transistor is forward biased (switched on), the voltage between base and emitter is approximately 0.6 V. Typical dc voltages for a 10 Vdc supply are: collector 7V, base 1.2V, emitter 0.6V.

Each component has a job: R1/R2 give base biasing, C1 is the input coupling capacitor, R3 is the collector load resistor, R4 provides emitter bias, C3 is the emitter bypass capacitor and C2 is the output signal coupling capacitor. A typical transistor amplifier circuit has a gain of between 100 and 150.

flashcards.back: With two P-N junctions, either N-P-N or P-N-P, rather than the single junction of a diode.

flashcards.front: Which transistor type is by far the most common?
When does an NPN transistor pass collector-emitter current?
flashcards.back: When the base voltage is 0.6V higher than the emitter voltage.

flashcards.front: What happens with 0V on the base of an NPN transistor?
flashcards.back: No current flows between the collector and emitter.

flashcards.front: What does R3 do in the NPN example circuit?
flashcards.back: It limits the current to prevent overload and produces a voltage drop that gives the output voltage Vout.

flashcards.front: How does a PNP transistor differ from an NPN?
flashcards.back: The dc supply potential is reversed, and the base must be 0.6V lower than the emitter for collector current to flow.

flashcards.front: How is a transistor biased for switching?
flashcards.back: Either fully off (no current flow) or fully on (maximum current flow).

flashcards.front: How is a transistor biased for amplification?
flashcards.back: 'Half on', with an alternating signal added to and subtracted from the dc bias at the base.

quiz.q: How many P-N junctions does a transistor have?
quiz.why: Instead of a single P-N junction, transistors have two junctions, N-P-N or P-N-P.

quiz.q: For an NPN transistor, what base voltage relative to the emitter allows collector current to flow?
quiz.why: When the base voltage is 0.6V higher than the emitter voltage, a current flows between collector and emitter.

quiz.q: For a PNP transistor, what must the base voltage be relative to the emitter?
quiz.why: A PNP uses a reversed supply and the base must be 0.6V lower than the emitter.

quiz.q: In the NPN example circuit, what produces the output voltage Vout?
quiz.why: R3 limits the current and produces a voltage drop that provides the output voltage Vout.

quiz.q: How is a transistor biased when it is used for switching?
quiz.why: In switching, the transistor is biased either off (no current) or fully on (maximum current).

quiz.q: How is a transistor biased when used for amplification?
quiz.why: For amplification the transistor is biased to be 'half on'.

quiz.q: What is the approximate base-emitter voltage when a transistor is forward biased?
quiz.why: When forward biased the base-emitter voltage is approximately 0.6 V.

quiz.q: In the typical amplifier on a 10 Vdc supply, what is the collector voltage?
quiz.why: Typical voltages are collector 7V, base 1.2V and emitter 0.6V.

quiz.q: In the amplifier circuit, what is C1?
quiz.why: C1 is the input coupling capacitor; C2 is the output coupling capacitor and C3 the emitter bypass.

quiz.q: What is the function of R4 in the transistor amplifier?
quiz.why: R4 provides emitter bias; R3 is the collector load resistor.

quiz.q: What gain does a typical transistor amplifier circuit have?
quiz.why: A typical transistor amplifier circuit has a gain of between 100 and 150.
